II.  Thesis  catholica  de  jure  proprietatis  exponitur  r. 

74.  Thesis :  Jus  dominii  privatum,  permanens  et  exclu- 
sivum  in  bona  externa,  etiam  fundos,  justis  limitibus 
circumscriptum,  legitimum  est,  a  jure  naturali  dimanat, 
ac  in  praesenti  statu  moraliter  necessarium  est. 

Declaratur  thesis.  (a)  Jus  dominii  prlvatum  :  agitur 
de  dominio  non  solum  utili,  sed  directo,  —  singulis  homini- 
bus,  non  autem  societati  competens;  non  negamus  societa- 
tem  ipsam  aliquot  bona  ut  propria  habere  posse,  sed  con- 
tendimus  privatos  cives  eodem  jure  gaudere. 

(b)  Permanens  et  exclusivum ;  jus  de  quo  agitur  non 
solum  modo  transitorio,  sed  etiam  modo  stabili  exerceri 
potest,  et  ad  haeredes  aliosve  transferri;  ita  proprium  est, 
ut  dominus  rei  ceteros  omnes  ab  ejus  possessione  excludere 
valeat. 

(c)  In  bona  externa,  i.  e.  sive  mobilia  sive  immobilia,  sive 
ad  novam  rerum  productionem,  sive  ad  usum  intendantur. 

75.  (d)  Justis  limitibus  circumscriptum  :  jus  enim  illud 
non  est  absolutum,  sed,  sicut  alia  jura,  limitatur,  et  quidem 
tripliciter  :  in  casu  extremo?  necessitatis,  quisque  occupare 
potest  id  quod  necessarium  est  ad  propriam  sustentatio- 
nem  (n.  446);  aliquando  etiam  bohum  commune  exigit  ut  do- 
minium  privatum  minuatur,  restringatur,  vel  tollatur  a 
Statu,  vi  alti  dominii  (nn.  123,  125,  131)  :  quod  tamen  fieri 

realise,  completent  1'ceuvre  syndicale  en  faisant  adherer  leur  Syndicat 
a  leur  Federation  locale  ou  Bourse  du  travail  et  par  le  canal  de  leur 
union  nationale  a  la  Confederation  Generale  du  Travail."

partibus  declarentur.

II.  De  dominio  semi-pleno  in  bona  externa. 

Dominium  plenum  complectitur  jus  disponendi,  fruendi 
et  alios  excludendi.  Jamvero  sub  hoc  triplici  respectu 
limitari  potest,  et,  quando  ita  limitatur,  restrictum,  seu 
semi-plenum  dicitur.

221.  i°  Notio  thesauri.  Thesaurus  definiri  potest  res

pantis.  Inventor  autem  merito  dicitur  qui,  sive  per  se,  sive 
per  alium  ad  hunc  finem  conductum,  primus  eum  detegit, 
seu  visibilem  reddit,  quamvis  nondum  eumdem  manu 
apprehenderit. 

Ratio  est  quia  thesaurus  speclari  nequit  ut  res  domini 
fundi,  cum  non  constet  eum  ab  ejus  majoribus  ibi  abscon-

sumptio  adest  thesaurum  a  progenitoribus  domini  absconditum

in  hoc  casu  in  conscientia  obligat,  etiam  ante  judicis  sententiam.

285.  i°  De  gravitate  injuriae.  Injuria  est  peccatum 
grave  ex  genere  suo,  quatenus  violat  jus  ex  se  gravis  mo-

Ad  dijudicandum  autem  utrum  injuria  sit  gravis  vel  non, 
ad  duo  attendendum  est  :  (a)  ad  singulos  liomines,  quorum 
jura  laeduntur,  utrum  videlicet  grave  nocumentum  seu  dam- 
num  eis  inferatur,  sive  materiale  sive  spirituale,  eorum 
libertatem,  securitatem  aut  pacem  turbando;  nam,  ut  recte 
ait  S.  Thomas,1"  peccata  quae  committuntur  in  proximum, 
sunt  pensanda  per  se  quidem  secundum  nocumenta  quae 
proximo  inferuntur,  quia  ex  hoc  habent  rationem  culpae  " ; 
(b)  ad  societatem  ipsam,  videlicet  ad  damnum  quod  bono 
publico  infertur,  aut  inferretur  si  impune  talis  injuria  com- 
mitteretur;  nam,  cum  bonum  commune,  ceteris  paribus, 
privato  praevaleat,  mortaliter  peccat  qui,  quamvis  leve  tan- 
tum  damnum  alicui  privato  intulerit,  graviter  rei  publicae 
nocet,  aut  noceret  posito  quod  ejus  a£tio  sub  gravi  non  pro- 
hiberetur;  ita  qui  centum  nummos  a  divite  subripit,  forsan 
nonnisi  leve  nocumentum  ei  affert;  peccat  tamen  mortali- 
ter,  quia,  posito  quod  tale  furtum  non  prohiberetur  sub 
gravi,  mox  societatis  ordo  subverteretur.

III.  De  officiis  ducum  ac  militum. 

359.  i°  Officia  utrisque  communia.  (a)  Tempore  justi  belli  duces 
ac  milites  patriae  inservire  tenentur,  etiam  cum  periculo  vitae,  quia 
bonum  publicum  id  postulat.  Unde  militiam  deserere  nequeunt, 
et  desertores  ad  castra  redire  debent;  qui  vero  ad  hostes  fugerent 
eisque  auxilium  quodcumque  praestarent,  proditores  essent  gravis- 
que  rei  sceleris. 

(b)  Si  bellum  sit  cerio  et  evidenter  infustum,  militare  non  licet, 
neque  hostes  m  praeno  occidere;  injusta  enim  aggressio  et  occisio 
innocentis  est  quid  intrinsece  malum.  Sed  in  praxi  raro  id  evenit; 
nam,  etiam  quando  belium  est  in  se  injustum,  plerumque  non  vide- 
tur  esse  tale  militibus,  qui  caeteroquin  de  legitimitate  belli  nec  solent, 
nec  possunt  generatim  inquirere  :  id  enim  relinquitur  supremae 
aucloritati  ac  Ccetui  Legislativo. 

(c)  In  dubio  utrum  bellum  sit  justum,  milites  jam  conducti,  aut 
aiias  sub  vexillis  suprema  auctoritate  vocati,  non  tenentur  de  legiti- 
mitate  belli  inquirere,  sed  praesumere  possunt  illud  esse  justum. 
Secus  dicendum  est  de  alienigenis  qui  sponte  exercitum  ingredi

laesi,  quod  aestimari  debet  judicio  viri  prudentis,  spectatis  omnibus 
circumstantiis  personae,  aetatis,  officii,  laboris,  etc. 

Quia  vero  difficile  est  ea  omnino  accurate  definire,  multum  expe- 
dit  ut  amica  compositio  seu  transaclio  fiat. 

(C)  Restitutio  fieri  debet  primario  ipsi personce  lcesce,  et,  post  ejus 
mortem,  ejus  hceredibus  proximis,  videlicet  parentibus,  liberis  et

et  filii  sibi  facile  subvenire  possunt;  nam  etiam  in  hoc  casu  inju- 
stum  damnum  passi  sunt.

hceredibus,  etiam  consanguineis,  et  creditoribus  defuncti,  qui  exinde

(a)  Non  clare  constat,  nec  proinde  urgenda  est  obligatio  resti-

habuerit  eos  ditandi,  ideoque  si  damnum  patiantur,  illud  per  acci-

citius  adeant  haereditatem.  —  Excipitur  tamen  casus  quo  quis  eorum

ejus  curam  agere  defunclus  implicite  saltem  promiserat,  et  ad  id 
sese  obligaverat. 

569."  (b)  Neque  constat  obligatio  restituendi  creditoribus  defundli, 
nisi  homicida  in  particulari  casu  praeviderit  et,  juxta  quosdam,

Notandum.  Si  lethaliter  vulneratus  sponte  ac  libere  ante  mortem. 
omnia  debita  homicidae  remittit,  hic  ex  stric~ta  justitia  ad  restitu-

§    I.    DE   CAUSIS   AD  TEMPUS   EXCUSANTIBUS. 

Causae  quae  ad  tempus  a  restitutione  excusant,  ad  duo

I.  De  impotentia,  quatenus  a  restitutione  excusat. 

Impotentia  duplex  est  :  physica  seu  absoluta,  et  moralis. 

600.  i°Principia.     (A)  Impossibilitas physica  seu  absoluta, 

—  quae  in  eo  consistit  ut  debitor  nihil  habeat  unde  resti- 
tuat,  quin  ad  extremam  necessitatem  se  reducat,  —  certo  a 
restitutione  excusat,  quamdiu  durat;  nam  ad  impossibile 
nemo  tenetur,  et  in  casu  extremae  necessitatis,  quisque  potest 
surripere,  et  a  fortiori  servare  ea  quae  necessaria  sunt  ad 
hanc  necessitatem  sublevandam;  dominus,  in  hoc  casu,  resti- 
tutionis  dilationi  non  rationabiliter  obstaret. 

(B)  Impossibilitas  moralis,  —  quando  quis  scilicet  resti- 
tuere  nequit  absque  gravi  damno  sive  proprio  sive  familiae, 

—  excusat  a  restitutione,  quamdiu  durat,  nisi  ex  dilatione 
dominus  similem  patiatur  necessitatem.  —  Etenim  lex  non 
obligat  cum  tanto  incommodo;  aliunde  dominus  non  est 
rationabiliter  invitus,  quando  vult  restitutionem  statim  fieri, 
quae  tantum  damnum  proximo  illatura  est.  —  Attamen,  si 
tum  dominus,  tum  debitor  irt  eadem  necessitate  gravi  ver- 
santur,  melior  esse  debet  conditio  domini,  qu,um  jus  habeat 
ad  usum  rei,  dum  debitor  tale  jus  non  habeat.  —  Si  vero 
debitor,  restituendo,  in  extremam  aut  quasi  extremam  ne- 
cessitatem  incideret,  dum  creditor  est  solum  in  gravi,  resti- 
tutio  differri  potest.

speciali  paclo,  v.  g.  solutionis  dilatio  ultra  tempus  a  lege  vel  con-

lum  omnes  quaestus  postea  faciendos;  posterior  autem  certas  res 
determinatas,  vel  illarum  usum,  aut  fructus  ex  eis  percipiendos,  vel 
determinatam  negotiationem.  Haec  multo  frequentior  est  quam 
societas  universalis. 

(B)  Societates  autem  particulares  alise  sunt  civiles  et  alise  commer- 
ciales  :  priores  ineuntur  quidem  ad  lucrum  faciendum,  sed  alio

domos  aedificandas,  ad  collegia  instituenda  et  administranda,  etc. ; 
commerciales  autem  dicuntur  quse  negotiationi  dant  operam. 

(C)  Sub  alio  respeclu,  societates  sunt  :  (a)  colleclivo  nomine  desi-

teneatur  de  omnibus  debitis  societatis;  ita,  v.  g.  Desclee,  Lefebvreet 
socii;  (b)  anonyma,  quando  socii  non  agunt  proprio  collectivo 
nomine,  sed  nomine  societatis  (Banque  de  France,  Credit Lyonnais), 
ita  ut  non  teneantur  de  debitis  ultra  portionem  capitalis  quam  con- 
tulerunt  aut  conferre  debuerunt. 3

pro  numeratd  pecunia  comparantur  aut  venduntur  quaedam  jura 
aut  merces. 

(B)  Tota  igitur  difficultas  versatur  circa  contraclus  ad  terminiiinj 
in  his  emuntur  aut  venduntur  valores  aut  merces,  ea  lege  ut  pretium 
solvatur  post  certum  tempus,  v.  g.  primo  vel  quintodecimo  die 
mensis  (qui  dies  liquidationis  dicitur),  et  quidem  pretium  quod  illo 
in  die  Bursa  vigebit.  Jamvero,  cum  hujusmodi  pretium  perpe- 
tuis  mutationibus  obnoxium  sit,  contraclus  est  aleatorius  et  vocatur 
speculatio  quaedam,  quia  uterque  contrahens  aliquid  lucrari  aut 
amittere  potest,  prout  pretium  majus  aut  minus  erit  die  liquida- 
tionis.  Hoc  autem  die  adveniente,  plerumque  non  traduntur  valo- 
res  aut  merces,  sed  solum  viclori  solvitur  dijferentia  inter  pretium 
quod  in  Bursa  die  emptionis  vigebat  et  illud  quod  viget  die  liqui- 
dationis.

IV.  De  officiis  medicorum  *. 
Medici  et  chirurgi    nobile    et  arduum    munus  exercent, 
cum  ipsis  cotnmittatur  vita  hominum  corporalis,  et  aliunde, 
christiane  officium  adimplendo,  non  parum  vitae  etiam  spi- 
rituali  conferre  valeant.

lere  debent;  secus  periculo  exponuntur  irreparabile  dam- 
num  aegrotis  aut  vulneratis  inferendi,  et  ex  hoc  capite  ad 
restitutionem  obligari  possunt.  Quia  vero  hodie  scientia 
medica  progreditur,  qui  suum  munus  fideliter  adimplere 
volunt,  studio  incumbere  non  desinant.  Pariter  in  difficil- 
limis  casibus,  quando  de  propria  peritia  dubitant,  alium 
medicum  peritiorem  advocare  non  dubitent,  si  aeger  aut  ejus 
familia  in  id  consentiat.

§  III.  De  quibusdam  oblectamentis  vitandis. 

1046.  Quaedam  oblectamenta  vitare  debent  clerici,  quia 
dignitatem  clericalem  dedecent,  aut  periculosa  sunt,  vel  scan- 
dalum  prsebent ;  ita  praesertim  venatio,  ingressus  in  tabemas, 
quidem  ludi,  chorece  et  spectacula. 

i°  De  venatione.  (A)  Respectu  juris  canonici,  tres  distinguuntur 
venationis  species  :  clamorosa,  quae  fit  magno  armorum  et  canum 
strepitu,  ad  capiendas  majores  feras,  nempe  apros,  cervos,  etc. ; 
quieta,  quae  fit  laqueis  et  retibus,  ad  capiendos  volucres,  lepores,  etc. ; 
quasi  intermedia,  quae  fieri  solet  adhibitis  quidem  armis  ignitis,  sed 
sine  magno  strepitu  et  cum  paucis  canibus. 

(B)  Jamvero  venatio  clamorosa  (cui  assimilatur  ea  quae  fit  cum 
falconibus  et  accipitribus)  clericis  etiam  minoribus  prohibita  est,  et 
quidem  per  se  sub  gravi  :  opponitur  enim  clericali  modestiae  et 
lenitati,  necnon  spiritui  religionis,  ob  vehementes  mentis  distrac- 
tiones  quae  ex  venatione  facile  oriuntur.  Quare,  in  libro  V 
DecretaL,  tit.  24,  De  Clerico  venatore,  c.  2,  legitur  :  "Omnibus 
servis  Dei  venatiories  et  silvaticas  vagationes  cum  canibus,  et 
accipitres  aut  falcones  interdicimus " ;  et  in  Codice,  c.  138, 
statuitur  ne  clerici  clamorosam  venationem  unquam  exer- 
ceant. 

(C)  Venatio  autem  quieta,  juxta  omnes,  clericis  licet.  Sed  de 
venatione  intermedia  dubitatur.  Benedictus  XIV  ut  probabi- 
liorem  habet  opinionem  quae  eam  illicitam  declarat,  quia  canones,

fraudes,  rixae  ex  cupiditate  vel  ex  timore  magni  damni.  Qui

summam  exponant,  per  se  graviter  peccant,  juxta  probabiliorem 
sententiam. 

(B)  Ludi  autem  industriales  aut  mixti,  qui  magis  a  solertia  quam

(b)  fntegra,  ita  ut  singula  verba  sine  mutilatione  seu  truncatione 
proferantur.  Si  mutilatio  ita  sit  notabilis  ut  sensus  multum  varietur,

puli,  nec,  in  casu  dubii,  officium  repetendum  est,  sed  attendendum 
est  ut  majori  cum  diligentia  postea  recitetur. 

1093.  Corollarium.  Licet  officium  recitare  non  solum  in  choro,  sed 
etiam  cum  socio,  quamvis  hic  ad  officium  non  teneatur.  Tunc  vero 
alternata  debet  esse  recitatio,  prout  fit  in  choro;  proinde,  si  tres 
sint  socii,  non  licet  ita  recitare,  ut  unus  dicat  primum,  alter  secun- 
dum,  et  alius  tertium  versum;  sed  socii  in  duos  veluti  choros  distri- 
bui  debent.  —  Requiritur  insuper  ut  se  mutuo  audiant;  si  tamen 
quis,  ad  alia  intentus,  aut  propter  strepitum,  vel  quia  socius  imper- 
fecle  pronuntiat,  paucanon  percipiat,  suae  obligationi  satisfacit,  nec 
tenetur  aliquid  repetere;  idem  dicendum  de  eo  qui,  dum  alii  reci- 
tant  in  choro,  aliquid  parare  debet  ad  officium  utile.  —  Recitatio 
ita  fieri  debet,  ut  unus  versus  non  incipiatur  priusquam  alter  abso- 
lutus  fuerit  :  secus  non  est  integra,  et  de  hac  mutilatione  idem 
dicendum  est  ac  supra.

De  opificum  conditione. 

1.  Rcrum  novarum  semel  excitata  cupidine,  qua?  diu  quidem 
commovet  civitates,  illud  erat  consecuturum  ut  commutationum 
studia  a  rationibus  politicis  in  ceconomicarum  cognatum  genus 
aliquando  defluerent.  —  Revera  i)  nova  industrice  incrementa  novis- 
que  euntes  itineribus  artes  :  2)  mutatce  dominorum  et  mercenario- 
rum  rationes  mutucB  :  3)  divitiarum  i?i  exiguo  numero  affluentia,  in 
multitudine  inopia  :  4)  opificum  cum  de  se  confidentia  maior,  tum 
inter  se  necessitudo  coniunctior,  praeterea  versi  in  deteriora  mores, 
effecere,  ut  certamen  erumperet.  In  quo  quanta  rerum  momenta 
vertantur,  ex  hoc  apparet,  quod  animos  habet  acri  expectatione 
suspensos  :  denique  ingenia  exercet  doctorum,  concilia  prudentum, 
conciones  populi,  legumlatorum  iudicium,  consilia  principum,  ut 
iam  caussa  nulla  reperiatur  tanta,  quae  teneat  hominum  studia 
vehementius.  —  Itaque,  proposita  Nobis  Ecclesiae  caussa  et 
salute  communi,  quod  alias  consuevimus,  Venerabiles  Fratres,

civitatum  constitutione  christiana,  aliisque  non  dissimili  genere, 
qu?e  ad  refutandas  opinionum  fallacias  opportuna  videbantur,  idem 
nunc  faciendum  de  conditione  opificum  '  iisdem  de  caussis  duxi-

gimus  :  in  his  tamen  Litteris  totam  data  opera  tractare  quaestionem 
apostolici  muneris  conscientia  monet,  ut  principia  emineant  quo- 
rum  ope,  uti  veritas  atque  aequitas  postulant,  dimicatio  dirimatur.

tarios,  eos  qui  rem,  et  eos  qui  operam  conferant,  inter  se  oportet 
contineri.  Periculosa  vero  contentio,  quippe  quae  ab  hominibus 
turbulentis  et  callidis  ad  pervertendum  iudicium  veri  concitan- 
damque  seditiose  multitudinem  passim  detorquetur.  Utcumque 
sit,  plane  videmus,  quod  consentiunt  universi,  infimae  sortis  homi- 
nibus  celeriter  esse  atque  opportune  consulendum,  cum  pars 
maxima  in  misera  calamitosaque  fortuna  indigne  versentur.

victu  domestico  apta  et  connexa  spectentur.  —  In  diligendo  genere 
vitae  non  est  dubium,  quin  in  potestate  sit  arbitrioque  singulorum 
alterutrum  malle,  aut  Iesu  Christi  sectari  de  virginitate  consilium, 
aut  maritali  se  vinclo  obligare.  Ius  coniugii  naturale  ac  primige- 
num  homini  adimere,  caussamve  nuptiarum  praecipuam,  Dei  auc- 
toritate  initio  constitutam,  quoquo  modo  circumscribere  lex  homi- 
num,  nulla  potest.  Crescite  et  muttipiicamini1.  En  igitur  familia, 
seu  societas  domestica,  perparva  illa  quidem,  sed  vera  societas, 
eademque  omni  civitate  antiquior;  cui  propterea  sua  quaedam  iura 
officiaque  esse  necesse  est,  quae  minime  pendeant  a  republica. 

Quod  igitur  demonstravimus,  ius  dominii  personis  singularibus 
natura  tributum,  id  transferri  in  hominem,  qua  caput  est  familiae, 
oportet  :  immo  tanto  ius  est  illud  validius,  quanto  persona  humana 
in  convictu  domestico  plura  complectitur.  Sanctissima  naturae  lex 
est,  ut  victu  omnique  cultu  paterfamilias  tueatur  quos  ipse procrearit : 
idemque  illud  a  natura  ipsa  deducitur,  ut  velit  liberis  suis,  quippe 
qui  paternam  referunt  et  quodam  modo  producunt  personam, 
acquirere  et  parare,  unde  se  honeste  possint  in  ancipiti  vitae  cursu 
a  misera  fortuna  defendere.  Id  vero  efficere  non  alia  ratione 
potest,  nisi  fructuosarum  possessione  rerum,  quas  ad  liberos  heredi- 
tate  transmittat.  Quemadmodum  civitas,  eodem  modo  familia,  ut 
memoravimus,  veri  nominis  societas  est,  quae  potestate  propria,  hoc 
est  paterna,  regitur.  Quamobrem,  servatis  utique  flnibus  quos 
proxima  eius  caussa  praescripserit,  in  deligendis  adhibendisque 
rebus  incolumitati  ac  iustae  libertati  suae  necessariis,  familia  quidem 
paria  saltem  cum  societate  civili  iura  obtinet.  Paria  saltem  dixi- 
mus,  quia  cum  convictus  domes/icus  et  cogitatione  sit  et  re  prior, 
quam  civilis  coniunctio,  priora  quoque  esse  magisque  naturalia  iura 
eius  officiaque  consequitur.  Quod  si  cives,  si  familiae,  convictus 
humani  societatisque  participes  factae,  pro  adiumento  offensionem, 
pro  tutela  diminutionem  iuris  sui  in  republica  reperirent,  fasti- 
dienda  citius,  quam  optanda  societas  esset. 

Velle  igitur  ut  pervadat  civile  imperium  arbitratu  suo  usque  ad 
intima  domorum,  magnus  ac  perniciosus  est  error.  —  Certe  si  qua

non  aliunde  quam  ex  opificum  labore  gigni  divitias  civitatum. 
lubet  igitur  aequitas,  curam  de  proletario  publice  geri,  ut  ex  eo, 
quod  in  communem  affert  utilitatem,  percipiat  ipse  aliquid,  ut 
tectus,  ut  vestitus,  ut  salvus  vitam  tolerare  minus  aegre  possit. 
Unde  consequitur,  favendum  rebus  omnibus  esse  quae  conditioni 
opificum  quoquo  modo  videantur  profuturae.  Quae  cura  tantum 
abest  ut  noceat  cuiquam,  ut  potius  profutura  sit  universis,  quia  non 
esse  omnibus  modis  eos  miseros,  a  quibus  tam  necessaria  bona 
proficiscuntur,  prorsus  interest  reipublicse.

cuiusquam  iniuria  potest.  Nihilominus  eis,  qui  imperant,  viden- 
dum  ut  communitatem  eiusque  partes  tueantur.  Communitatem 
quidem,  quippe  quam  summae  potestati  conservandam  natura 
commisit  usque  eo,  ut  publicae  custodia  salutis  non  modo  suprema 
lex,  sed  tota  caussa  sit  ratioque  principatus  :  partes  vero,  quia 
procurationem  reipublicae  non  ad  utilitatem  eorum,  quibus  com- 
missa  est,  sed  ad  eorum,  qui  commissi  sunt,  natura  pertinere, 
philosophia  pariter  et  fides  christiana  consentiunt.  Cumque  impe- 
randi  facultas  proficiscatur  a  Deo,  eiusque  sit  communicatio  quae- 
dam  summi  principatus,  gerenda  ad  exemplar  est  potestatis  divinae, 
non  minus  rebus  singulis  quam  universis  cura  paterna  consulentis.

35«  Quoad  ad  tutelam  bonorum  corporis  et  externorum,  primum 
omnium  eripere  miseros  opifices  e  saevitia  oportet  hominum  cupi- 
dorum,  personis  pro  rebus  ad  quaestum  intemperanter  abutentium. 
Scilicet  tantum  exigi  operis,  ut  hebescat  animus  labore  nimio, 
unaque  corpus  defatigationi  succumbat,  non  iustitia,  non  huma- 
nitas  patitur.  In  homine,  sicut  omnis  natura  sua,  ita  et  vis  efficiens 
certis  est  circumscripta  finibus,  extra  quos  egredi  non  potest. 
Acuitur  illa  quidem  exercitatione  atque  usu,  sed  hac  tamen  lege  ut 
agere  intermittat  identidem  et  acquiescat.  De  quotidiano  igitur 
opere  videndum  ne  in  plures  extrahatur  horas,  quam  vires  sinant. 
Intervalla  vero  quiescendi  quanta  esse  oporteat  ex  vario  genere 
operis,  ex  adiunctis  temporum  et  locorum,  ex  ipsa  opificum  valetu- 
dine  iudicandum.  Quorum  est  opus  lapidem  a  terra  excindere, 
aut  ferrum,  aes,  aliaque  id  genus  effodere  penitus  abdita,  eorum 
labor,  quia  multo  maior  est  idemque  valetudini  gravis,  cum  brevi- 
tate  temporis  est  compensandus.  Anni  quoque  dispicienda  tempora  : 
quia  non  raro  idem  operae  genus  alio  tempore  facile  est  ad  toleran- 
dum,  alio  aut  tolerari  nulla  ratione  potest,  aut  sine  summa  difficul- 
tate  non  potest.  —  Denique  quod  facere  enitique  vir  adulta  aetate 
beneque  validus  potest,  id  ^feminapuerove  non  est  cequum  postu- 
lare.  Immo  de  pueris  valde  cavendum,  ne  prius  officina  capiat, 
quam  corpus,  ingenium,  animum  satis  firmaverit  aetas.  Erum- 
pentes  enim  in  pueritia  vires,  velut  herbescentem  viriditatem, 
agitatio  precox  elidit :  qua  ex  re  omnis  est  institutio  puerilis  interi- 
tura.  Sic  certa  quaedam  artificia  minus  apte  conveniunt  in  feminas 
ad  opera  domestica  natas  :  quae  quidem  opera  et  tuentur  magno- 
pere  in  muliebri  genere  decus,  et  liberorum  institutione  prosperi- 
tatique  familiae  natura  respondent.  Universe  autem  statuatur, 
tantum  esse  opificibus  tribuendum  otii,  quantum  cum  viribus  compen- 
setur  labore  consumptis ;  quia  detritas  usu  vires  debet  cessatio 
restituere.  In  omni  obligatione,  quae  dominis  atque  artificibus 
invicem  contrahatur,  haec  semper  aut  adscripta  aut  tacita  conditio 
inest,  utrique  generi  quiescendi  ut  cautum  sit ;  neque  enim  hones- 
tum  esse  convenire  secus,  quia  nec  postulare  cuiquam  fas  est,  nec 
spondere  neglectum  officiorum,  quae  vel  Deo  vel  sibimetipsi  homi- 
nem  obstringunt.

INTRODUCTION.2 

In  England,  as  well  as  in  tbie  United  States  of  America,  law  is 
of  two  kinds  :  international  and  municipal;  the  former  is  that  rule 
of  civil  conducl:,  which  is  prescribed  by  the  common  consent  of 
Christian  nations,  and  regulates  their  intercourse  with  one  another; 
the  latter  is  that  rule  of  civil  conduct,  which  is  prescribed  by  the 
supreme  power  in  a  State,  and  regulates  the  intercourse  of  the  State 
with  its  subjecls  and  of  those  subjecls  with  each  other.  —  Here  we 
have  to  deal  only  with  Municipal  law. 

In  either  country,  Municipal  law  is  unwritten  or  written.  Unwrit- 
ten  law,  known  also  as  customary  law,  or  comtnon  law,  is  that  which 
originated  in  the  common  wisdom  and  experience  of  society,  in 
time  became  an  established  custom,  and  has  finally  received  judicial 
sanclion  in  the  decision  of  the  courts  of  last  resort.  Written  law  is 
that  which  has  been  directly  prescribed,  in  so  many  words,  by  the 
supreme  power  of  the  State. 

In  America,  municipal  law  is  of  two  kinds  :  Federal  law,  which 
is  enacled  by  the  supreme  power  in  the  United  States,  and  regu- 
lates,  in  matters  of  a  national  character,  the  intercourse  of  the 
federal  government  with  the  people,  and  of  the  people  with  each 
other  or  with  citizens  of  foreign  States  ;  —  State  /aw,  which  is 
enacted  by  the  supreme  power  in  each  individual  State,  and  regu- 
lates,  in  all  matters  not  of  a  national  character,  the  intercourse  of 
such  State  with  its  own  people  and  of  its  people  among  themselves. 
—  From  this  it  follows  that  State  laws  are  not  the  same  throughout 
the  Union,  and  that  it  is  well  for  a  priest  to  get  a  certain  knowledge 
of  the  statutes  of  his  own  State;  but,  in  the  most  intricate  cases,  it 
may  be  necessary  to  consult  with  a  skilful  and  honest  lawyer.

I.     The  Copyright  law. 

By  copyright  we  understand  the  right  of  an  author  to  print  and 
publish  his  own  original  work,  exclusively  of  all  other  persons. 

i°  In  England, x  the  copyright  Acl,  1842  (5  et  6  Vict.  c.  45)  provides 
that  the  copyright  of  every  book,  —  under  which  word  is  included 
every  volume,  part  or  division  of  a  volume,  pamphlet,  sheet  or  letter- 
press,  sheet  of  music,  map,  chart,  or  plan  separately  published  in 
the  United  Kingdom,  —  which  shall  be  published  in  the  lifetime 
of  its  author  (whether  a  subject  of  the  king  or  not)  shall  endure 
for  his  natural  life>  and  for  sevenyears  longer;  or,  if  the  seven  years 
shall  expire  before  the  end  of  forty-two  years  from  the  first  publi- 
cation,  shall  endure  for  such  period  oiforty-two  years ;  and  that, 
when  the  work  is  posthumous,  the  copyright  shall  endure  for  forty- 
two  years  from  the  first  publication,  and  shall  belong  to  the  pro- 
prietor  of  the  author's  manuscript ;  and  that,  as  regards  articles 
which  are  first  published  in  periodical  works,  the  copyright,  unless 
there  is  some  agreement  to  the  contrary,  remains  vested  in  the 
author.  The  proprietor  of  a  copyright  infringed,  by  the  book  being 
unlawfully  printed  within  the  British  dominions,  may  claim  damages 
for  the  injury  already  suffered,  and  an  injunction  to  prevent  the 
continuance  of  the  infringement  or  piracy;  as  regards  books 
unlawfully  reprinted  in  any  place  out  of  the  British  dominions,  and 
imported  into  the  United  Kingdom,  they  may  be  seized  as  forfeited, 
by  any  officer  of  the  customs  or  excise,  and  the  offenders  are  liable 
to  penalties. 

Moreover  by  the  International  Copyright  Acls,  it  is  provided 
that  His  Majesty  by  order  in  council  may,  —  as  regards  books, 
prints,  articles  of  sculpture,  paintings,  drawings,  photographs  and 
other  works  of  art,  first  published  in  a  foreign  country,  — allow  the 
respecl:ive  authors,  inventors,  artists,  and  their  personal  representa 
tives,  privilege  of  copyright  for  any  period  not  exceeding  the  term 
for  which  the  like  produclions  would  be  protected,  if  first  published 
in  the  United  Kingdom. 

20  In  the  United  States,  the  Act  of  March  3,  1891,  provides  that  the 
author,  inventor,  designer  or  proprietor  of  any  book,  map,  chart, 
dramatic  or  musical  composition,  engraving,  cut,  print,  or  photo- 
graph  or  negative  thereof,  or  of  a  painting,  drawing,  chromo, 
statuary,  and  of  models  or  designs  intended  to  be  perfected  as 
works  of  the  fine  arts;  and  the  executors,  administrators,  or  assigns 
of  any  such  person,  shall,  upon  complying  with  the  provisions  ot 
this  chapter,  have  the  sole  liberty  of  printing,  reprinting,  publishing, 
completing,  copying,  executing,  finishing  and  vending  the  same : 
and,  in  the  case  of  a  dramatic  composition,  of  publicly  performing

or  representing  it,  or  causing  it  to  be  performed  or  represented  by 
others.  Authors  and  their  assigns  have  the  exclusive  right  to 
translate  or  to  dramatize  any  of  their  works. 

(A)  Conditions  to  be  complied  with.  (a)  But  to  secure  this  privilege 
books  must  be  printed  from  type  set  or  plates  made  in  the  United 
States;  photographs  from  negatives  made  in  the  United  States;

stantial  changes  are  made  shall  be  deposited  in  the  office  of  the 
Librarian  of  Congress.  —  No  copyright  is  valid  unless  notice  is 
given  by  inserting  in  every  copy,  on  the  title-page  or  the  page 
following,  these  words  :  "  Entered  according  to  Act  of  Congress, 
in  the  year  —  by  —  in  the  office  of  the  Librarian  of  Congress,  at 
Washington  ";  or  "  Copyright,  19  —  by.  — 

(c)  In  the  case  of  books  published  in  more  than  one  volume,  or 
of  periodicals  published  in  numbers,  a  copyright  must  be  entered 
for  each  volume,  or  part  of  a  book,  or  number  of  a  periodical.  To 
complete  the  copyright  on  a  book  published  serially  in  a  periodical, 
two  copies  of  each  serial  part,  as  well  as  of  the  complete  work,  \i 
published  separately,  should  be  deposited. 

(d)  Foreign  authors  may  acquire  copyright  by  complying  with 
the  foregoing  regulations. 

(B)  Duration.  The  original  term  of  copyright  runs  for  twenty-eight 
years.  Within  six  months  before  the  end  of  that  time,  the  author 
or  designer,  or  his  widow  or  children  may  secure  a  renewal  for  the 
further  term  of  fourteen  years,  making  forty-two  in  all.  Within  two 
months  from  date  of  renewal  the  record  thereof  must  be  advertised 
in  an  American  newspaper  for  four  weeks. 

II.     Patent  right. 

Patent-right  is  a  privilege  granted  by  the  State  to  the  tirst  inventor 
of  any  new  contrivance,  that  he  alone  shall  be  entitled,  during  a 
limited  period,  to  benefit  by  his  own  invention. 

iu  In  England,  the  applicant  for  a  patent  may  be  a  British  subject 
or  a  foreigner.    (a)  The  application  is  made  by  petition  contained 


4*  PATENT   RIGHT. 


in,  and  supported  by,  a  solemn  declaration  that  the  petitioner  is  the 
true  and  first  inventor,  and  that  the  invention  is  not  in  use  in  Great 
Britain  by  any  other  person,  to  the  best  of  his  knowledge  and  belief; 
it  must  be  accompanied  by  either  a  provisional  or  a  complete  speci- 
fication  :  in  this  latter  case,  the  complete  specification  must  be 
sent  no  later  than  nine  months  from  the  date  of  the  application. 

(b)  The  objecl;  of  patent  must  be  a  new  manufaflure  within  the 
realm  of  England,  that  is  some  article  fabricated  by  the  hand  of 
man,  or  an  addition,  by  way  of  improvement,  to  one  already 
existing,  or  a  chemical  process  of  production,  it  must  be  new  in 
Great  Britain,  but  the  previous  notoriety  of  the  article,  in  a  foreign 
country,  is  no  objection  to  the  validity  of  the  patent. 

(c)  The  patent-right  can  be  granted  only  to  the  true  and  first 
inventor  :  no  one  can  claim  this  characler,  if  it  appear  that  the 
novelty  in  question  was  first  suggested  to  him  by  some  other  person 
in  England. 

(d)  It  is  granted  for  fourteen  years,  and  this  term  may  be  extended 
for.  seven,  or,  in  exceptional  cases,  fourteen  years,  in  favour  of  a 
patentee  who  has  not  reaped  the  full  benefit  of  his  invention. 

(e)  Ii  a  patent-right  be  infringed,  the  inventor  may  claim  damages 
for  the  injuries  sustained,  and  obtain  an  order  restraining  the 
wrongdoer  from  the  further  use  of  the  invention. 

2°  In  America,  patents  are  issued  in  the  name  of  the  United 
States,  and  under  the  seal  of  the  Patent  Oftice,  to  any  person  who 
has  invented  or  discovered  any  new  and  useful  art,  machine,  manu- 
facture,  or  composition  of  matter  or  any  new  and  useful  improve- 
ment  thereof,  not  known  or  used  by  others  in  this  country,  and 
not  patented  or  described  in  any  printed  publication  in  this  or  an) 
foreign  country,  before  his  invention  or  discovery  thereof,  and  not 
in  public  use  or  on  sale  for  more  than  two  years  prior  to  his  appli- 
cation,  unless  the  same  is  proved  to  have  been  abandoned ;  and  by 
any  person  who,  by  his  own  industry,  genius,  efforts  and  expense 
has  invented  and  produced  any  new  and  original  design  for  amanu- 
facture,  bust,  statue,  alto-relievo,  or  bas-relief ;  any  new  and  original 
design  for  the  printing  of  woolen,  silk,  cotton,  or  other  fabrics;  any 
new  and  original  impression,  ornament,  pattern,  print,  or  picture  to 
be  printed,  painted,  cast,  or  ortherwise  placed  on  or  worked  into  any 
article  of  manufacture ;  or  any  new,  useful,  and  original  shape  or 
configuration  of  any  article  of  manufacture,  the  same  not  having 
been  known  nor  used  by  others  before  his  invention  or  production 
thereof,  nor  patented  nor  described  in  any  printed  publication,  upon 
payment  of  the  fees  required  by  law  and  other  due  proceedings  had. 
(a)  Every  patent  contains  a  grant  to  the  patentee,  his  heirs  or 
assigns,  for  the  term  of  seventeen  years,  of  the  exclusive  right  to

make,  use,  and  vend  the  invention  or  discovcry  throughout  the 
United  States  and  the  Territories,  referring  to  the  specification  for

If  it  appear  that  the  inventor,  at  the  time  of  making  his  appli- 
cation,  believed  himself  to  be  the  first  inventor  or  discoverer,  a 
patent  vvill  not  be  refused  on  account  of  the  invention  or  discovery,

(b)  Joint  inventors  are  entitled  to  a  joint  patent;  neither  can

patent  for  their  separate  invention  :  nor  does  the  fact  that  one 
furnishes  the  capital  and  another  makes  the  invention  entitle  them 
to  make  application  as  joint  inventors;  but  in  such  case  they  may 
become  joint  patentees. 

(c)  The  receipt  of  letters  patent  from  a  foreign  government  will 
not  prevent  the  inventor  from  obtaining  a  patent  in  the  United 
States,  unless  the  invention  shall  have  been  introduced  into  public 
use  in  ^he  United  States  more  than  two  years  prior  to  the  applica- 
tion.  But  every  patent  granted  for  an  invention  which  has  been 
previously  patented  by  the  same  inventor  in  a  foreign  country  will 
be  so  limited  as  to  expire  at  the  same  time  with  the  foreign  patent, 
or,  if  there  be  more  than  one,  at  the  same  time  with  the  one  having 
the  shortest  unexpired  term,  but  in  no  case  will  it  be  in  force  more 
than  seventeen  years. 

(d)  Applications  for  a  patent  must  be  made  in  writing  to  the  Com- 
missioner  of  Patents.  The  applicant  must  also  file  in  the  Patent 
Office  a  written  description  of  the  same,  and  of  the  manner  and 
process  of  making,  constructing,  compounding,  and  using  it,  in  such 
full,  clear,  concise,  and  exact  terms  as  to  enable  any  person  skilled 
in  the  art  or  science  to  which  it  appertains,  or  with  which  it  is  most 
nearly  connected,  to  make,  construct,  compound,  and  use  the  same  ■ 
and  in  case  of  a  machine,  he  must  explain  the  principle  thereof, 
and  the  best  mode  in  which  he  has  contemplated  applying  that  prin- 
ciple,  so  as  to  distinguish  it  from  other  inventions,  and  particularly 
point  out  and  distinctly  claim  the  part,  improvement,  or  combi- 
nation  which  he  claims  as  his  invention  or  discovery.  The  speci- 
fication  and  claim  must  be  signed  by  the  inventor  and  attested  by 
two  witnesses. 

When  the  nature  of  the  case  admits  of  drawings,  the  applicant 
must  furnish  a  drawing  of  the  required  size,  signed  by  the  inventor 
or  his  attorney  in  fact,  and  attested  by  two  witnesses,  to  be  filed  in 
the  Patent  Ornce.  In  all  cases  which  admit  of  representation  by 
model,  the  applicant,  if  required  by  the  Commissioner,  shall  furnish 
a  model  of  convenient  size  to  exhibit  advantageously  the  several 
parts  of  his  invention  or  discovery.

(e)  The  applicant  shall  make  oath  that  he  verily  believes  himself 
to  be  the  original  and  first  inventor  or  discoverer  of  the  art,  machine, 
manufacture,  composition,  or  improvement  for  which  he  solicits  a 
patent,  that  he  does  not  know  and  does  not  believe  that  the  same 
was  ever  before  known  or  used,  and  shall  state  of  what  country  he 
is  a  citizen.  Such  oath  may  be  made  before  any  person  within  the 
United  States  authorized  by  law  to  administer  oaths,  or,  when  the 
applicant  resides  in  a  foreign  country,  before  any  minister,  charge 
d'affaires,  consul,  or.  commercial  agent  holding  commission  under 
the  Government  of  the  United  States. 

(f )  On  the  filing  of  such  application  and  the  payment  of  the  fees 
required  by  law,  if,  on  such  examination,  it  appears  that  the 
claimant  is  justly  entitled  to  a  patent  under  the  law,  and  that  the 
same  is  sufficiently  useful  and  important,  the  Commissioner  will 
issue  a  patent  therefor. 

Every  patent  or  any  interest  therein  shall  be  assignable  in  law  by 
an  instrument  in  writing;  and  the  patentee  or  his  assigns  or  legal 
representatives  may,  in  like  manner,  grant  and  convey  an  exclusive 
right  under  his  patent  to  the  whole  or  any  specified  part  of  the 
United  States. 

(g)  A  reissue  is  granted  to  the  original  patentee,  his  legal  repre- 
sentatives,  or  the  assignees  of  the  entire  interest  when,  by  reason 
of  a  defective  of  insufncient  specification,  or  by  reason  of  the 
patentee  claiming  as  his  invention  or  discovery  more  than  he  had 
a  right  to  claim  as  new,  the  original  patent  is  inoperative  or  invalid, 
provided  the  error  has  arisen  from  inadvertence,  accident,  or 
mistake,  and  without  any  fraudulent  or  deceptive  intention.  In  the 
cases  of  patents  issued  and  assigned  prior  to  July  8,  1870,  the  appli- 
cations  for  reissue  may  be  made  by  the  assignees;  but  in  the  cases 
of  patents  issued  or  assigned  since  that  date,  the  applications  must 
be  made  and  the  specifications  sworn  to  by  the  inventors,  if  they 
be  living. 

III.     Of  things  real  and  personal. 

Property,  as  to  its  legal  character,  is  of  two  kinds  :  real  and 
personal.  Things  real  (otherwise  called  real property  or  realty)  are 
such  as  are,  in  contemplation  of  law,  pennanent  and  inwwvable  as 
lands,  houses,  etc.  Things  personal  (or  personal  property,  or 
chattels)  are  those  which,  in  contemplation  of  law,  are  movable  and 
have  not  a  permanent  duration,  such  as  jewels,  watches,  books,  etc; 
they  are  called  persona/,  because  they  may  attend  the  owner's 
person,  wherever  he  goes.  —  Some  introduce  a  third  distinction, 
viz.  mixed  things,  which  partake  of  the  nature  of  both,  as  deeds  to 
an  estate;  these  are  called  real  by  others,  because  they  may  be 
considered  as  something  accessory  to  real  property. 


OF  THINGS  REAL  AND  PERSONAL.       7* 

i°  Of  things  real. '  Real  property  CQnsists  in  /ands,  tenements  and 
hereditaments. 

(A)  First  it  consists  of  lands  and  of  whatever  is  erected,  or 
growing  upon,  or  affixed  thereto,  including  whatever  is  beneath  or 
above  the  surface.  By  way  of  exception,  houses,  trees,  growing 
crops  might  be  personalty,  for  instance,  if  a  house  were  built  on 
the  land  of  another,  with  the  latter's  consent.  Again  objects,  in 
their  nature  real,  may  by  severance  from  the  realty,  become  per- 
sonal;  thus  trees  growing  on  the  land  are  real;  when  cut,  and  lying 
in  logs  on  the  land,  they  are  personal.  On  the  other  hand,  an 
object,  which  considered  in  itself,  is  personal,  may  become  real;  so 
the  materials  pf  which  a  house  is  to  be  built,  are  personal;  but, 
when  constructed  into  a  building,  may  become  real ;  again  a  great 
many  fixtures,  though  originally  movable  and  personal,  become  real 
by  being  affixed  to  reai  estate. 

(B)  It  consists  also  of  tenements;  which  word  includes  not  only 
houses  and  buildings,  but  whatever  may  be  holden,  provided  it  be 
of  a  permanent  nature,  as  a  grade  in  the  army,  offices,  rents,  etc. 

(C)  Hereditaments,  which  pertain  also  to  real  property,  include 
whatever  may  be  inherited,  be  it  corporeal  or  incorporeal :  (a)  cor- 
poreal  hereditaments  include  land  and  everything  permanently 
affixed  to  it;  (b)  an  incorporeal  hereditament  is  a  right  issuing  out 
of  a  thing  corporate,  or  concerning  or  annexed  to,  or  exercised 
within  the  land  in  the  ownership  of  another,  such  as  the  right  of 
way,  or  the  right  of  one  man  to  pass  and  repass  over  the  land  of 
another  by  some  accustomed  or  designated  path. 

2°  Of  things  personal.  -  Things  or  chattels  personal  comprise 
in  a  general  way  all  sorts  of  things  moveable.  They  consist  of 
inanimate  things,  as  goods,  plate,  money ;  or  of  vegetable  productions, . 
as  the  fruit  or  plant  when  severed  from  the  ground;  also  of  animals, 
which  can  convey  themselves  from  one  spot  to  another;  lastly  of 
certain  incorporeal  rights  in  moveables,  such  as  patent-right, 
copyright,  the  right  to  a  trade-mark. 

Chattels  personal  may  be  either  mpossession,  or  else  in  action  :  — 
in  possession,  when  a  man  has  the  enjoyment,  actual  or  constructive, 
of  the  thing;  —  in  action,  when  a  man  has  not  the  enjoyment  of 
it,  but  merely  a  right  to  recover  it  by  action,  or  by  course  of  law  : 
thus,  money  due  on  a  bond  is  a  chattel  (or  chose)  in  action,  because, 
though  not  actually  possessed,  it  may  be  recovered  by  course 
of  law. 


Stephen,  vol.  I,  p.  168-638  ;  Robi?ison,  Elementary  Law,  §  38  —  §  93. 
Stephen,  vol.  II,  p.  1-12;  Robinson,  Elem.  Law,  §  113-118. 


8*  OF   PARENT   AND   GHILD. 

IV.     Of  Parent  and  child. J 

Children  are  legitimate,  when  begotten  or  born  in  wedlock ;  ille- 
gitimate,  when  begotten  and  born  out  of  wedlock.  The  legal  pre- 
sumption  is  that  a  child  born  during  wedlock  is  legitimate;  this  pre- 
sumption  may  be  rebutted,  but  only  by  clear  proof.  In  England, 
one  born  a  bastard  is  not  rendered  legitimate  by  the  subsequent 
marriage  of  his  parents;  but,  in  many  States  of  the  Union,  sub- 
sequent  marriage  legitimates  a  child  previously  born.  —  Here  we 
treat  only  of  legitimate  children. 

i°  Duties  of  parents.  Parents  are  bound  to  protect,  maintain  and 
educate  their  children  : 

(a)  To  protect,  viz.  to  uphold  a  child  in  his  law-suits  and  defend 
him  against  an  unjust  assailant. 

(b)  To  maintain  minor  children;  but  this  obligation  extends  only 
to  necessaries ;  and  the  father  is  not  obliged  to  support  his  children 
in  idleness  if  they  are  able  to  work.  He  is  obliged  by  law  to  main- 
tain  them,  even  though  they  have  some  property  of  their  own;  but 
this  rule  has  been  relaxed  by  courts,  when  the  estate  of  children  is 
larger  than  that  of  parents.  —  After  the  father's  death,  the  mother 
is  bound  to  support  the  child,  if  able,  but  not  at  her  expense,  if  the 
child  has  property  of  his  own.  —  As  a  rule,  the  capital  of  his  pro- 
perty  will  not  be  infringed  for  his  support,  except  when  necessary. 
—  The  parents  are  not  liable  for  the  debts  of  their  children,  even 
for  necessaries,  except  when  these  have  beeh  bought  with  their 
parents  actual  or  implied  authority. 

(c)  To  educate  their  children,  according  to  their  condition;  but 
this  duty  does  not  extend  to  a  trade  or  profession. 

2°  Rig-hts  of  parents.  Parents  have  a  right  to  the  custody  and  ser- 
vices  of  their  minor  children. 

(A)  Custody.  At  common  law,  the  father  has  the  paramount  right 
to  the  custody  of  the  minor  child,  and,  before  dying,  may  appoint 
a  testamentary  guardian;  in  case  of  the  father's  death  without  the 
exercise  of  this  power,  the  mother  succeeds  to  these  rights,  but  she 
loses  them  by  remarriage.  —  The  right  of  custody  may  be  forfeited 
by  misconduct,  and  granted  to  the  mother  or  to  a  third  person. 

(B)  Services.  The  father  has  the  right  to  his  children's  services 
and  earnings,  whilst  they  live  with  him  and  are  maintained  by  him ; 
he  may  voluntarily  relinquish  this  right  by  express  or  implied  eman- 
cipation,  which  gives  the  child  the  free  disposition  of  his  own  time 
and  wages  and  discharges  the  parent  from  obligation  to  support, 

1  Stephen.  vol.  II,  p.  289-304;  Browne,  Elements  of  the  law  of  domestic 
relations,  Boston,  1890,  p.  70-89 ;  Robinson,  Elements  of  American  Juris- 
prudence,  Boston,  1900,  §  26. 


OF   GUARDIAN    AND    WARD. 


unless  the  child  becomes  unable  to  support  himself.  —  But  the 
father  has  no  right  in  the  chilcTs  separate  personal  or  real  estate; 
its  management  is  entrusted  to  guardians  or  trustees  appointed  by 
the  will  of  the  donor  of  the  property,  or  by  a  competent  court. 

The  parent  has  a  right  of  action  for  expenses  and  loss  of  the 
child's  services  caused  by  the  negligence  or  wrong  of  another;  this 
right  is  not  defeated  by  the  fact  that  the  child  is  living  with  and  in 
the  service  of  another,  unless  the  parent  has  relinquished  all  right 
to  the  child's  service.  —  Again  the  father,  or  after  his  death  the 
mother,  has  a  right  of  action  for  enticing  away  or  abducting  the 
child,  but  not  for  enticing  him  into  a  marriage;  the  theory  of  this 
action  is  reimbursement  for  loss  of  service,  not  compensation  for 
wrong  to  the  child ;  the  principle  is  the  same  in  an  action  for  seduc- 
tion  of  a  daughter. 

The  parent  is  not  liable  for  his  child's  torts,  although  committed 
in  his  presence,  but  without  his  approval;  he  is  liable  for  injury  by 
the  child's  negligent  acts  which  he  knows  of  and  permits  on  his 
premises. 

V.     Of  guardian  and  ward. l 

At  common  law,  an  infa?it  or  minor  is  any  person,  male  or  f emale, 
under  twenty-one  years  of  age.  But,  in  the  United  States,  some 
statutes  have  reduced  the  age  required  for  majority.  Infants  being 
generally  unable,  because  of  their  youth  and  inexperience,  to  take 
care  of  their  own  interests,  are  placed  under  guardianship. 

There  are  four  kinds  of  guardians  :  (a)  guardians  by  nature  and 
?iurture,  who  are  the  parents  themselves,  first  the  father,  and  on 
his  death  the  mother;  (b)  testamentary  guardians,  who  are  appointed 
by  the  father's  last  will;  (c)  guardians  appointed  by  the  Court, 
when  an  infant,  having  some  property,  was  entrusted  to  no  other 
guardian;  (d)  guardians  ad  litem,  who  are  appointed  by  a  court  of 
justice  to  prosecute,  or  more  commonly  to  defend,  for  an  infant  in 
any  action  or  litigious  proceeding  therein  pending,  to  which  such 
infant  may  be  a  party.2 

i°  Rigths  and  duties  of  guardians.  (A)  With  regard  to  the  person 
qf  the  ward :  the  guardian  is  entitled  to  the  custody  of  the  ward's 
person,  subject  to  the  regulation  of  the  court;  his  right  is  even 
superior  to  that  of  the  parent,  if  this  be  alive;  but  as  a  rule  the 
parent  is  appointed  guardian,  unless  unfit.  —  Hence  the  guardian 
may  recover  the  person  of  the  ward  from  one  unlawfully  detaining 
him,  select  the  place  of  his  education,  and  bind  him  to  appren- 
ticeship. 


1  Stephen,  vol.  II,  p.  305-316;  Browne,  Domestic  relations,  p.  90-122. 

2  With  regard  to  guardianship  in  socage,  by  electio?i,  or  by  custom, 
allen  in  disuse,  see  Stephen,  1.  c.  p.  310-314.

He  is  bound  to  maintain  him,  but  only  from  the  warcTs  own 
estate.  He  has  a  large  discretion  in  expenditure  not  encroaching 
on  the  capital,  but  is  not  allowed  to  expend  more  than  the  income 
of  his  ward's  estate  without  consent  of  the  court,  except  in  the  case 
of  imperative  and  sudden  necessity;  in  which  case  he  may  use  the 
principal  of  personalty,  but  cannot  sell  the  real  estate  except  by 
order  of  the  court  and  for  the  purpose  of  maintenance.  —  If  neces- 
sary,  he  may  place  the  ward  at  work,  or  if  he  is  too  young  and 
feeble,  entrust  him  to  some  charitable  institution.  —  As  he  has  no 
right  to  his  ward's  services,  he  cannot  recover,  for  his  own  profit,  any 
compensation  for  injuries  committed  against  the  ward. 

(B)  As  to  the  ward's  estate,  the  guardian  is  bound  to  manage  it  as 
a  good  and  faithful  administrator  :  he  must  receive,  collect  and 
invest  the  income,  pay  the  necessary  expenses  of  his  ward,  and 
account  for  his  trust;  he  may  lease,  discharge  a  mortgage,  sue  for 
debts,  compromise,  release,  or  submit  to  arbitration.  He  cannot 
by  general  contract  bind  his  ward's  estate,  nor  avoid  a  beneficial 
contract  made  by  his  ward.  He  has  no  right  to  purchase  the  ward's 
property  or  sell  his  own  property  to  his  ward.  He  may  lease  the 
real  estate  of  the  ward,  and  repair  it,  but  must  not  make  improve- 
ments  without  authority  of  the  court;  with  regard  to  selling  real 
estate,  special  formalities  are  required. 

In  the  discharge  of  all  these  duties,  the  guardian  must  act  with 
care  and  diligence,  and  is  responsible  for  fraud  and  negligence; 
but,  when  he  has  acted  in  good  faith,  according  to  his  best  judgment 
and  with  ordinary  care,  he  will  not  be  strictly  held  for  losses. 

The  guardian  cannot  reap  any  personal  benefit  from  his  ward's 
estate  except  what  is  allowed  by  court  for  his  services. 

2°  Rights  of  the  ward.  The  ward  may  restrain  his  guardian  from 
committing  waste.  —  On  the  termination  of  the  guardianship,  he 
may  sue  him  for  an  accounting,  within  a  reasonable  time.  He  will 
ahvays  receive  the  aid  of  the  court  in  recovering  property  embezzled, 
concealed  or  conveyed  away  in  fraud  of  his  rights. 

A  gift  or  conveyance  from  ward  to  guardian  during  or  shortly 
after  majority  is  presumed  fraudulent,  and  will  not  be  sustained 
except  on  the  clearest  proof  of  the  utmost  good  faith. 

An  infant  may  bind  himself  by  contract  for  necessaries;  but  most 
of  the  other  contracts  made  by  him  are  considered  as  voidable. 

VI.     Of  husband  and  wife.1 

Under  the  ancient  rules  of  the  common  law,  the  wife's  personality 
was  suspended  and  merged  in  that  of  her  husband,  with  whom  she 
became  in  law  one  person,  and  that  person  the  husband.     All  her

personal  property  which  she  had  in  her  possession  at  the  date  of 
the  marriage,  instantly  became  the  property  of  the  husband,  and  all 
her  claims  and  rights  of  action  against  others  vested  in  him,  to  be 
collected  by  him  and  applied  to  his  own  use,  if  he  chose.  Her 
temporary  interests  in  lands,  the  rents  and  profits  of  her  real  estate, 
and  all  her  services  and  earnings  during  the  time  of  coverture  (that 
is  until  the  marriage  relation  was  legally  dissolved)  were  also  his. 

But  in  more  recent  times,  both  in  England  and  America,  these 
disabilities  of  married  women  have  been  greatly  modified,  first  by 
the  action  of  courts  of  equity,  and  next  by  legislative  enactment. 

i°  In  England,  the  matter  has  been  mostly  settled  by  the  Married 
Women  Property  Acts  of  1870  and  1882.  According  to  these  sta- 
tutes,  every  woman  who  marries  on  or  after  the  first  day  of  January, 
1883,  is  to  hold  as  her  separate  estate  all  her  property,  either  then 
already  belonging  to  her  or  afterwards  coming  to  her  in  any  manner, 
whether  such  property  be  real  or  personal,  including  wages,  earnings, 
and  gains  earned  or  made  by  her  in  any  occupation  which  she  car- 
ries  on  separately  from  her  husband.  —  Besides  a  wife,  whenever 
married,  may  effect  an  insurance  upon  her  own  or  her  husband's 
\\le,for  her  separate  use,  and  may  also  acquire  property  independ- 
ently  of  her  husband  in  such  deposits  as  she  shall  have  made  in  a 
savings  bank,  or  other  bank,  or  as  she  shall  have  invested  in  the 
funds,  in  a  joint-stock  company,  or  in  an  industrial  or  loan  society, 
—  provided  that  she  shall  not  have  used  her  husband's  moneys 
without  his  consent,  and  shall  not  have  deposited  or  invested  such 
moneys  in  fraud  of  his  creditors.  —  Again,  if  a  wife  be  deserted  by 
her  husband  without  reasonable  cause,  she  may  obtain  an  order, 
which  is  called  a  protection  order,  under  which  any  money  or  pro- 
perty  she  shall  acquire  by  her  own  lawful  industry,  or  become  pos- 
sessed  of,  after  the  desertion,  will  be  protected  and  belong  to  her 
as  if  she  were  &feme  sole  (unmarried);  and  if  a  wife  \%judicially  sepa- 
rated  from  her  husband,  she  is  to  be  deemed  &feme  sole  as  regards 
all  her  property  acquired  subsequently  to  the  judicial  separation. 

If  she  survives  her  husband,  she  is  entitled  to  dower,  that  is  to 
hold  to  herself,  for  the  term  of  her  natural  lif e,  the  third  part  of  all 
the  lands  and  tenements  of  which  her  husband  was  seized  or 
possessed  in  f ee  simple  or  fee  tail  at  any  time  during  the  coverture, 
and  of  which  any  issue  that  she  might  have  had  could  have  been 
heir.

married  before  or  after  certain  dates,  and  sometimes  different

married  woman  retains  the  ownership,  administration  and  enjoyment 
of  her  own  real  or  personal  property  as  if  she  were  &fe?ne  so/e,  or 
unmarried.  Hence,  she  may  bargain,  sell,  assign  and  transfer  her 
personal  property,  —  perform  any  services  or  labor,  carry  on  any 
trade  or  business  on  her  sole  and  separate  account,  and  her  earnings 
therefrom  shall  be  her  sole  and  separate  property.  She  may  sue 
and  be  sued  in  all  matters  pertaining  to  her  separate  property,  for

husband,  except  for  those  contracted  by  her  as  his  agent  for  the 
support  of  herself  and  her  children.  The  husband  is  not  liable  for 
his  wife's  ante-nuptial  debts  except  to  the  amount  of  her  separate 
property  acquired  by  him ;  nor  for  contracts  made  by  her  respecting 
her  separate  property,  unless  it  relates  to  property  given  or  granted 
by  him. 

Many  States  by  statute  permit  the  wife  to  have  the  benefit  of  an 
insurance  on  the  husband's  life  as  against  his  creditors,  though  he 
has  paid  the  premiums  with  his  own  money. 

In  some  States  of  the  Union,  not  only  the  widow,  but  also  the 
husband,  at  the  death  of  his  wife,  has  the  right  of  dower;  x  so,  in 
Maryland,  according  to  the  new  law  of  1898,  "  every  husband  shall 
acquire,  by  virtue  of  his  marriage,  an  estate  for  his  life  in  one  third 
of  the  lands  held  or  owned  by  his  wife  at  any  time  during  the  mar- 
riage,  whether  by  legal  or  equitable  title . . .  but  such  estate  shall  not 
operate  to  the  prejudice  of  any  claim  for  the  purchase  money  of 
such  lands,  or  other  liens  on  the  same  ".  Yet  this  right  of  dower 
may  be  relinquished  by  either  husband  or  wife,  by  joint  or  separate 
deed,  according  to  the  statutes  of  the  various  States. 

VII.     Of  Corporations. 2 

i°  Notion.  A  corporation  is  a  body  consisting  of  one  or  more 
persons,  established  by  or  under  the  authority  of  the  law,  with  the 
capacity  of  succession,  either  perpetual  or  for  a  limited  period,  and 
the  faculty  of  acting  as  a  natural  person.  —  It  may  consist  of  one 
member,  who  is  then  a  corporatio?i  sole;  thus  every  bishop  in 
England,  and  a  few  bishops  in  America,  are  acknowledged  as 
corporation  sole  for  their  respective  diocese.  But  generally  corpo- 
ration  consist  of  several  members.  —  Corporations  are  public, 
when  created  by  law  to  promote  public  interests,  such  as  counties, 

1  Dower,  in  english  law,  is  the  right  of  the  widow  to  the  use  and 
enjoyment,  for  her  life,  of  one-third  of  all  the  real  estate  of  the 
deceased  husband  which  the  children  could  have  inherited. 

-  Stepiicn,  vol.  III,  p.  2-55;  Robinson,  American  Jurisprudence, 
§  71-112. 


OF    PRESGRIPTION.  13: 

towns,  cities;  or  private,  when  created  for  the  private  benefit  of  the 
members,  such  as  banks,  joint-stock  companies,  universities,  etc. 

2°  Organisation.  Formerly  a  charter,  granted  by  Parliament  or 
by  the  Legislature  of  the  State,  was  required  for  any  new  corpo- 
ration.  But  now,  in  most  of  the  States  of  the  Union,  a  corporation 
may  be  formed  by  complying  with  some  conditions  determined 
by  the  Statutes  of  each  State.  As  a  rule,  articles  of  incorporation 
have  to  be  drawn  up  and  signed  by  a  certain  number  of  persons, 
determining  the  name,  the  object,  the  place  of  business,  the  amount 
of  capital  or  stock,  the  names  and  residences  of  stock-holders 
and  of  directors;  these  articles  are  deposited  with  and  filed  in 
the  proper  ofifice;  and  from  this  moment  the  corporation  has  a  legal 
existence. 

So  a  corporation  must  have  a  name  by  which  it  may  make  con- 
tracts  and  hold  property,  sue  and  be  sued ;  it  must  have  a  corporate 
seal  to  be  aflfixed  to  the  documents,  and  a  place  of  business  for  the 
general  management  of  affairs.  It  has  the  right  of  perpetual  suc- 
cession,  by  appointing  new  members  and  ofificers. 

3°  Dissolution.  A  corporation  may  be  dissolved  in  various  ways  : 
by  the  death  of  all  its  members,  if  new  ones  have  not  been  elected ; 
by  the  voluntary  consent  of  its  members;  by  expiration  of  the  time 
determined  by  the  statutes,  if  limited;  by  a  law  repealing  the 
charter,  if  created  by  an  act  of  the  Legislature;  by  a  decree  of 
forfeiture  for  misuse  of  non-user  of  its  privileges. 

VIII.     Of  prescription. 

In  Great  Britain  as  well  as  in  America,  there  is  a  distinction  to 
be  made  between  prescription  and  limitation  at  law. 

i°  Of  prescription  properly  so  called. x  In  British  countries  as  well 
as  in  the  United  States,  prescription  proper  applies  only  to  incor- 
poreal  hereditaments  and  to  certain  exemptions  and  privileges ;  land 
or  moveables  cannot  be  claimed  by  prescription.  Incorporeal 
hereditaments  include,  among  other  species,  the  right  of  way,  the 
right  of  fishing,  the  right  to  water  cattle  at  a  spring,  or  pond  or 
stream,  the  right  of  pasture,  the  right  to  lay  pipes  to  conduct 
water  or  gas,  the  right  to  put  up  a  wall  or  a  fence  on  the  land  of 
an  adjacent  proprietor,  and  also  rents,  ofifices,  dignities,  franchises 
and  the  like.  —  Prescription  is  always  founded  on  the  actual  pos- 
session  of  the  thing  in  question,  and  the  measure  of  the  actual 
enjoyment  is,  as  a  rule,  the  measure  of  the  right.  The  ti?ne,  during 
which  such  possession  must  have  continued,  was  determined,  in 
England,  by  the  Prescription  Act,  1832,  and  is  of  twenty,  thirty, 
forty  and  sixty  years  according  to  some  distinctions  which  it  would 

1  Stephen,  vol.  I,  p.  595-638;  Robinson,  Elem.  Law,  §  132. 


14*  OF   PRESCRIPTION. 


be  too  long  here  to  explain;  —  in  the  United  States,  it  is  fixed  by 
statute,  and  extends  usually  to  twenty  years. 

In  either  country,  the  possession  must  have  been  :  (a)  adverse, 
i.  e.  inconsistent  with  the  enjoyment  of  the  corporeal  property  by  lts 
true  owner;  (b)  under  a  rtaim  ofright;  i.  e.  with  the  avowal  on  the 
part  of  the  possessor,  that  he  has  a  real  right  to  the  possession  of 
the  incorporeal  hereditament ;  (c)  peaceable  and  continuous,  i.  e. 
without  such  action,  on  the  part  of  the  owner  of  the  corporeal  pro- 
perty,  as  suspends,  or  restricts  or  interferes  with  the  enjoyment 
of  the  hereditament  by  its  possessor;  also  without  abandonment,  or 
disuse  on  the  part  of  the  possessor;  and  therefore  enjoyed  during 
the  whole  of  the  required  period  of  time  by  the  same  individual 
possessor,  or  by  a  series  of  individuals,  each  claiming  a  title 
through  his  predecessors ;  (d)  with  the  knowledge  of  the  owner  of 
the  corporeal  property. 

20  Of  the  limitation  of  actions.  Besides  prescription,  by  which  a 
right  may  be  acquired,  there  is  another  privilege,  called  limitation 
at  laiv,  whereby  the  claimant  of  a  right  cannot,  after  a  certain 
period,  enforce  his  claim  before  a  court  of  justice. 

The  statuUs  of  limitation  originated  in  England  as  far  back  as 
1623,  and  were  adopted  in  most  of  the  States  of  the  Union. 

In  Great  Britain,1  the  statutes  of  limitation  apply  both  to  raz/and 
personal  property. 

(A)  The  realproperty  Limitation  Act,  1874,  completing  and  cor- 
recting  the  statutes  previously  enacted,  decides  :  (a)  that  no  person 
shall,  after  ist  January  1879,  make  entry  or  distress  upon,  or  bring 
an  action  to  recover  any  land  or  rent,  unless  within  tivelve  years 
next  after  the  time  at  which  the  right  to  make  such  entry  or  distress, 
or  to  bring  such  action,  shall  have  first  accrued  to  the  person 
making  or  bringing  the  same.  However  if,  at  the  time  at  which  the 
right  of  any  person  shall  first  accrue,  such  person  is  under  the 
disability  of  infancy,  coverture,  idiocy,  lunacy  or  unsoudness  of 
mind,  he  or  the  person  claiming  through  him  may,  though  twelve 
years  have  expired,  enter  or  sue  within  six  years  next  after  the 
person  to  whom  the  right  accrued  shall  have  died  or  ceased  to  be 
under  disability;  but  no  such  right  of  entry,  distress  or  ac.Hon,  shall 
be  exercised,  except  within  thirty  years  next  after  the  right  accrues, 
even  though  the  disability  may  have  attached  during  the  whole  of 
the  thirty  years,  or  although  the  term  of  six  years  above  mentioned 
shall  not  have  yet  expired. 

(b)  That  no  action  or  other  proceeding  shall  be  brought  to 
recover  any  money  secured  by  any  mortgage,  judgment,  or  lien,  6r 
otherwise  charged  upon  or  payable  out  of  any  land  or  rent  at  law 
or  in  equity,  or  any  legacy,  except  within  twelve  years  next  after  a 

1  Stephen,  vol.  III,  p.  508-525. 


OF    PRESCRIPTION.  15* 

present  right  to  receive  the  same  shall  haveaccrued  to  some  persor 
capable  of  giving  a  discharge  for  or  release  of  the  same,  —  unless 
indeed  part  of  the  principal  money  shall  have  been  paid  or  an 
acknowledgment  in  writing  given,  and  then  only  within  twelve 
years  after  such  payment  6r  acknowledgment. 

(c)  That  no  arrears  of  rent,  or  of  interest,  or  any  damages  in 
respecl  of  any  such  arrears,  shall  be  recoverable,  but  within  six 
years  after  the  same  shall  have  become  due  or  been  acknowledged 
in  writing  to  the  person  entitled  thereto  or  his  agent,  signed  by  the 
party  chargeable  or  his  agent,  —  subjecl;  to  this  proviso,  that  where 
a  prior  mortgagee  or  incumbrancer  has  been  in  possession,  within 
one  year  next  before  aclion,  the  second  mortgagee  may  in  his 
action  recover  the  arrears  of  his  interest  for  the  whole  period 
(although  exceeding  six  years)  that  the  priormortgagee  has  been  in 
possessiori. 

(B)  With  regard  to  things  personal,  it  is  provided,  in  substance  : 
(a)  that  aclions  of  trespass  in  general,  all  aclions  of  account  (other 
than  between  merchants),  and  all  aclions  of  debt  on  simple  contracl, 
or  for  arrears  of  rent  not  due  upon  specialty,  shall  be  limited  to 
six  years  after  the  cause  of  aclion  accrued;  (b)  that  acStions  of 
trespass  for  the  particular  injuries  of  assault,  menace,  battery, 
woundingand  imprisonment,  shall  belimited  to four  years ;  (c)  and 
the  aclions  on  the  case  for  verbal  slander,  shall  be  limited  to 
two  years.  —  But  to  these  limitations,  there  are  exceptions,  in 
favour  of  persons  labouring  under  disability. 

N.  B.  Between  these  two  classes  of  limitations,  there  is  this 
important  difference,  namely,  that  the  former  statute  concerning 
realproperty  has,  by  its  express  provision,  the  effect  of  extinguishing 
the  right,  as  well  as  of  barring  the  remedy;  whilst  the  latter,  con- 
cerning  personalty,  bars  the  remedy  only,  without  extinguishing  the 
right,  so  that  though  I  can  bring  no  aclion  to  recover  a  debt  on 
contract,  after  the  expiration  of  the  limited  period,  there  is  nothing 
to  prevent  my  obtaining  payment  of  the  debt  after  that  period  in 
any  other  manner.  —  This  distinclion  is  particularly  important  for 
theforum  conscientice. 

In  the  United  States,  the  matter  is  regulated  by  statutes  which 
substantially  agree  with  the  english  regulations  as  above  explained. 
However,  in  many  States,  the  period  of  time  during  which  an 
action  may  be  brought  to  recover  real  property,  is  iwenty  years,  as 
it  used  to  be  in  England  before.  —  Besides,  in  some  States,  special 
laws  have  been  enacted  allowing  squatters  sooner  to  become  owners 
of  the  lands  they  have  cultivated  in  good  faith.

(C)  These  untrue  conclusions  may  have  been  induced  by  repre- 
sentations  of  the  other  party  made  with  a  knowledge  of  their 
untruth  and  with  the  intention  of  deceiving  :  this  isfraud.  The 
person  injured  by  fraud  has  several  remedies  :  (a)  he  may  affirm 
the  contract  and  ask  for  a  fulfilment  of  its  terms,  or  damages  for 
such  loss  as  he  has  sustained  by  their  non-fulfilment;  (b)  he  may 
avoid  the  contract,  either  by  taking  active  steps  to  get  it  cancelled 
on  the  ground  of  fraud,  or  by  resisting  as  uit  for  specific  perform- 
ance,  or  an  action  for  damages  brought  in  respect  of  it;  (c)  if,  after 
becoming  aware  of  the  fraud,  he  does  not  give  notice  of  his  inten- 
tion  to  avoid  the  contract,  he  may  lose  his  option  to  affirm  or  avoid 
the  contract,  but  he  retains  the  right  of  entering  an  action  for  deceit 
and  of  recovering  by  that  means  such  damage  as  he  has  sustained. 

(D)  The  consent  of  one  of  the  parties  may  have  been  extorted  from 
him  by  the  other  by  actual  or  threatened/mwza/violence  T :  this  is 
duress.  A  contract  entered  into  under  duress  is  not  void  ipso  facto, 
but  is  voidable. 

(E)  Circumstances  may  render  one  of  the  parties  morally  incapa- 
ble  of  resisting  the  will  of  the  other,  so  that  his  consent  is  no  real 
expression  of  intention  :  this  is  undue  influence.  Contracts  made 
under  such  an  influence  are  voidable,  not  void.  As  soon  however 
as  the  undue  influence  is  entirely  withdrawn,  the  contract  may  be 
reaffirmed  by  the  influenced  party  and  thus  become  valid. 

4°  Of  the  subject-matter  of  contracts.  The  subject-matter  of  a  con- 
tract  may  be  either  some  real  or  personal  estate,  or  some  exercise 
of "  skill  and  labor,  or  some  right  or  some  forbearance  of  an  existing 
right,  or  any  other  matter  beneficial  to  the  person  to  whom  it  is  to 
be  given,  or  for  whom  it  is  to  be  done.  But  certain  objects  of 
contract  are  forbidden  or  discouraged  by  law. 

(A)  Some  contracts  are  forbidden  by  Statute;  thus  certain  wagers 2 
have  been  declared  to  be  void,  in  England,  by  the  Gaming  Act  of 
1845,  enacting  :  "  that  all  contracts  or  agreements,  whether  by  parole 
or  in  writing,  by  way  of  gaming  or  wagering,  shall  be  null  and  void ; 
and  that  no  suit  shall  be  brought  or  maintained  in  any  Court  of  Law 

1  It  is  considered  to  be  personal,  when  the  subject  of  it  is  the  con. 
tracting  party  himself,  or  his  wife,  parent,  or  child. 

-  A  wager  is  a  promise  to  give  money  or  money's  worth  upon  the  de- 
termination  or  ascertainment  of  an  uncertain  event ;  wagers,  or  wager- 
ing  contracts,  made  by  a  man  to  protect  himself  against  a  risk  (marine 
insurance,  life  insurance)  are  perfectly  lawful ;  but  wagers  made  entirely 
for  sport  or  gambling  are  forbidden.

or  Equity  for  recovering  any  sum  of  money  or  valuable  thing  alleged 
to  be  won  upon  any  wager,  or  which  shall  have  bcen  deposited  in 
the  hands  of  any  person  to  abide  the  event  on  which  any  wager 
shall  have  been  made  ". 

(B)  Other  contracts  are  illegal  at  Common  laiv;  such  are  agree- 
ments  to  commit  a  crime,  an  indictable  offence,  or  a  civil  wrong; 
agreements  to  injure  the  public  service,  or  to  pervert  the  course  of 
justice;  agreements  which  are  contrary  to  good  morals.1 

N.  B.  The  effect  of  illegality  upon  the  validity  of  contracts  varies 
according  to  circumstances;  it  may  affect  the  whole  or  only  a  part 
of  the  contract;  the  contract  may  be  simply  discouraged,  in  as  much 
as  the  law  will  not  enforce  it,  or  made  void.  (a)  When  the  contract 
is  divisible,  i.  e.  when  you  can  sever  the  illegal  from  the  legal  part, 
you  may  reject  the  bad  part  and  retain  the  good;  but  where  you 
cannot  sever  them,  the  contract  is  altogether  void.  (b)  From  the 
text  of  the  law,  it  must  be  considered  whether  the  contract  is  for- 
bidden  under  penalty,  without  being  declared  void,  —  or  whether  it 
is  simply  discouraged,  but  without  any  penalty,  —  or  whether  it  is 
purely  and  simply  made  void.2 

5°  Of  the  parties  to  a  contract.  Any  person,  not  debarred  therefrom 
by  law,  may  make  a  contract.  Now  certain  persons  are  by  law  incap- 
able,  wholly  or  in  part,  or  binding  themselves  by  a  promise,  or  of 
enforcing  a  promise  made  to  them.  This  incapacity  may  arise  from 
political  or  professional  status,  —  from  youth,  —  from  the  marriage 
bond,  —  from  permanent  or  temporary  aberration  of  mind. 

(A)  Fro?7i  political  or  professional  status  :  (a)  An  alien  cannot 
acquire  property  in  a  British  ship.  —  An  alien  enemy  cannot,  with- 
out  licence  from  the  Crown,  make  any  fresh  contract  or  enforce  any 
existing  contract  during  the  continuance  of  hostilities;  but  his  rights 
as  to  contracts  made  before  the  commencement  of  war  are  only  sus- 
pended,  and  can  be  enforced  upon  the  conclusion  of  peace.  —  A 
person  convicted  of  treason  or  felony  cannot,  whilst  undergoing

X.     Of  the  contract  of  sale. ' 

The  contract  of  sale  is  a  contract  by  which  the  property  in  goods 
is  transferred  from  one  person  to  another  for  a  price.  Where  this 
price  is  money,  it  is  a  sale  proper ;  where  it  is  goods,  it  is  called 
exckange  or  barter.  Again  there  is  a  difference  between  a  sale  and 
an  agreement  to  sell :  where  the  property  in  the  goods  is  transferred 
from  the  seller  to  the  buyer,  the  contract  is  called  a  sale;  but 
where  the  transfer  is  to  take place  at  some  future  time,  or  subject  to 
some  condition  thereafter  to  be  fulfilled,  it  is  an  agreement  to  sell. 

—  To  constitute  a  sale,  the  goods  sold  must  be  specific,  i.  e.  suffi- 
ciently  determined,  —  in  a  deliverable  state,  and  the  sale  must  be 
unconditional;  if  any  one  of  these  requisites  is  missing,  the  contract 
is  only  an  agreement  to  sell. 

i°  In  Great  Britain,  the  contract  of  sale  is  now  regulated  by  the 
sale  of  Goods  Act,  1893;  we  shall  give  a  brief  summary  of  the  main 
points  contained  therein. 

(A)  With  regard  to  the  transfer  of  property  :  (a)  In  the  case  of  a 
ssdefor  ready  money,  of  specific  goods,  immediately  deliverable,  the 
property  in  the  goods  is  transferred,  as  soon  as  the  price  is  agreed 
upon  by  the  two  parties,  provided  one  of  these  three  conditions  is 
fulfilled  :  1)  delivery  of  the  goods  or  of  any  portion  of  them,  by  way 
of  earnest,  or  tender  of  delivery,  —  2)  payment  or  tender  of  payment, 

—  3)  if  any  part  of  the  price  be  paid  down  and  accepted.  —  (b)  In 
the  case  of  a  sale  of  goods  on  credit,  i.  e.  when  the  goods  are  to  be 
delivered  forthwith,  but  to  be  paid  afterwards,  the  property  passes 
to  the  vendee  immediately  upon  the  striking  of  the  bargain,  without 
either  delivery  of  the  goods  on  the  one  hand,  or  tender  of  payment 
on  the  other.  —  (c)  Where  there  is  a  contract  for  the  sale  of 
unascertained  goods  (i.  e.  not  specific),  the  property  passes  not 
until  the  particular  goods  are  ascertained  or  made  specific  by 
weighing  out,  or  by  severance  or  otherwise.  —  (d)  Where  the  goods 
are  not  in  a  deliverable  state,  the  property  remains  in  the  vendor  and 
at  his  risk;  sometimes,  as  in  the  case  of  ships  which  are  being 
built  under  a  contract  to  pay  piecemeal  as  certain  parts  of  the 
vessel  are  completed,  the  property  passes  piecemeal  from  the  vendor 
into  the  vendee. 

(B)  With  regard  to  the  right  of  possession.     Even  in  the  case  of  a 
sale  of  specific  and  finished  goods,  the  vendee  cannot  take  the

(a)  "  Subject  to  the  provisions  of  this  Act,  where  goods  are  sold 
by  a  person  who  is  not  the  owner  thereof,  and  who  does  not  sell  1 
them  under  the  authority  or  with  the  consent  of  the  owner,  the 
buyer  acquires  no  better  title  to  the  goods  than  the  seller  had, 
unless  the  owner  of  the  goods  is  by  his  conduct  precluded  from 
denying  the  seller's  authority  to  sell 

(b)  Where  goods  are  sold  in  market-overt,x  according  to  the  usage 
of  the  market,  the  buyer  acquires  a  good  title  to  the  goods,  provided 
he  buys  them  in  good  faith  and  without  notice  of  any  defect  or 
want  of  title  on  the  part  of  the  seller. . . 

(c)  When  the  seller  of  goods  has  a  voidable  title  thereto,  but  his 
title  has  not  been  avoided  at  the  time  of  the  sale,  the  buyer  acquires 
a  good  title  to  the  goods,  provided  he  buys  them  in  good  faith  and 
without  notice  of  the  seller's  defect  of  title. 

(d)  Where  goods  have  been  stolen  and  the  offender  is  prosecuted

tative,  notwithstanding  any  intermediate  dealing  with  them,  whether 
by  sale  in  market-overt  or  otherwise...
