4°  Legal  forms  of  wills.  Two  kinds  of  wills  are  recognised  by  law  : 
nuncupative  sind/ormaL  A  ?iuncupative  will  is  an  oral  will  declared 
by  a  testator  before  witnesses,  and  afterwards  reduced  to  writing;  it 
is  valid  when  made  by  a  soldier  in  actual  military  service,  —  i.  e. 
engaged  in  an  expedition,  —  or  a  sailor  at  sea,  or,  in  some  States, 
by  other  people  in  extremis  who  are  prevented  from  executing  a 
formal  will.  But,  apart  from  these  exceptional  cases,  all  wills  must 
be  in  writing. 

(A)  In  England x  :  (a)  No  will  is  valid,  unless  it  be  in  writing,  and 
signed  at  the  foot  or  end  thereof  by  the  testator  or  some  other  per- 
son,  in  his  presence,  and  by  his  direction,  such  signature  being  also 
made  or  acknowledged  by  him,  in  the  presence  of  two  or  more  wit- 
nesses,  present  at  the  same  time,  and  such  witnesses  attesting  and 
subscribing  the  will  in  his  presence.  According  to  the  new  statutes, 
the  incompetency  of  any  attesting  witness  will  not  invalidate  the 
will;  yet,  any  beneficial  gift  to  an  attesting  witness,  or  to  the 
husband  or  wife  of  an  attesting  witness,  remains  void. 

(b)  As  to  revocation,  no  will  shall,  under  the  new  statute,  be  revok- 
ed  by  the  marriage  alone  of  a  testator  or  testatrix.  A  revocation 
may,  however,  take  place  by  the  execution  of  another  will  or  of  a 
codicil,  or  of  some  writing  of  revocation  executed  like  a  will,  or  by 
the  burning,  tearing,  or  other  destruction  of  the  original  will  by  the 
testator  or  by  some  person  in  his  presence  and  by  his  direction ;  — 
obliteration  and  other  alteration  made  after  execution  are  of  no 
effect,  where  the  original  meaning  can  still  be  deciphered,  unless 
executed  with  the  same  ceremonies  as  the  will  itself,  or  the  signature 
of  the  testator  and  the  subscription  of  the  witnesses,  be  made  oppo- 
site  or  near  the  part  altered,  or  at  the  foot  or  end  of  some  merao- 
randum  written  on  the  will,  and  referring  to  the  alteration. 

(c)  When  a  will  is  once  revoked,  it  is  not  to  be  revived  othenvise 
than  by  re-execution  of  the  original,  or  by  a  codicil  duly  executed 
and  showing  an  intention  of  revival. 

(B)  In  the  United  States,  the  same  rules  are  substantially  enforced 
with  a  few  exceptions  introduced  by  statute-laws.  (a)  So,  in  a  very 
few  States,  holograph  wills  are  allowed :  they  must  be  entirely  writ- 
ten,  dated  and  signed  by  the  testator's  own  hand,  and  when  it  is  so, 
no  subscribing  witnesses  are  required. 

(b)  But,  in  most  of  the  States,  two  or  three  witnesses  are  required  : 
any  one  may  be  a  witness  who  is  competent  to  give  testimony,  and 
is  not,  on  the  other  hand,  beneficially  interested  in  the  will.    If  the 

1  Stephen,  1.  c.  p.  551-554. 


OF    LAST    WILLS    AND    TESTAMENTS.  27* 


will  is  not  written  by  the  testator,  but  by  another  person,  this  person 
shall  write  his  own  name  as  a  witness,  in  the  presence  of  two  other 
witnesses;  —  besides,  the  testator  shall  write  his  full  name  at  the  end 
of  the  will,  —  or,  if  he  does  not  know  how  to  write,  he  will  make  a 
cross  or  any  other  mark.  —  It  is  not  necessary  that  the  witnesses 
should  know  the  contents  of  the  will;  but  the  testator  must 
acknowledge,  in  their  presence,  his  signature,  and  declare  that  this 
paper  is  his  last  will  and  testament.  Then  the  will  is  to  be  signed 
by  them,  in  presence  of  the  testator  and  in  the  same  room;  in  some 
States,  the  simultaneous  presence  of  all  the  witnesses  is  required. 
If  the  witnesses  cannot  sign,  a  cross  or  other  mark  will  suffice.  They 
should  also  write  out  their  addresses,  though  this  is  not  necessary 
fcr  the  validity  of  the  testament.  —  A  codicil,  i.  e.  any  new  disposi- 
tion  added  to  the  will,  is  subject  to  the  same  legal  forms  as  the 
will  itself. 

(c)  As  a  rule,  a  will  is  revoked  by  marriage  and  the  birth  of  a  child 
subsequent  to  the  writing  of  the  will,  if  the  wife  and  child  were 
wholly  unprovided  fcr;  but  marriage  alone  will  not,  in  most  of  the 
States,  break  off  the  will.  It  may  be  also  revoked  by  the  destruc- 
tion  of  the  original  will,  or  execution  of  another  will,  as  explained 
above,  p.  26. 

5°  Of  the  executors  or  administrators  of  the  will.  It  is  well  for  the 
testator  to  appoint  an  executor  of  the  will;  otherwise,  the  Court  will 
provide  for  it  by  appointing  an  administrator.  The  appointment  of 
an  executor  may  be  qualified  by  limitations  as  to  time,  place  and 
subject  matter,  and  the  appointment  may  be  conditional.  —  As  a 
rule,  any  one  capable  of  making  a  will  may  be  an  executor.  In  some 
States,  minors  may  be  named  as  executors,  but  they  cannot  act  if 
they  are  under  twenty-one  years  of  age  when  the  testator  dies.  In 
most  States,  a  single  woman  may  now  be  an  executor;  and,  under 
modern  statutes,  married  women  may  also,  in  many  States,  act  as 
executors,  without  any  assent  an  the  part  of  their  husbands. 

The  duty  of  an  executor,  after  burying  the  deceased  party,  is  to 
b&ve  the  will  proved  in  the  proper  Court,  and,  af ter  probate,  to  make 
an  inventory  of  the  property, x  which  must  be  filed  within  a  stated 
period  in  the  register's  office.  Then  he  will  administer  the  property 
according  to  the  directions  of  the  will  and  the  laws  of  the  State. 
Where  there  is  a  deficiency  of  assets,  if  there  are  no  directions  in 
the  will  on  the  subject,  personal  property  is  generally  to  be  used 
first  to  pay  debts  with,  and  real  property  afterwards. 

1  By  way  of  exception,  an  inventory  may  not  be  necessary,  where 
the  testator  makes  the  executor  the  residuary  legatee.  But,  in  this 
case,  if  there  is  not  property  enough  to  pay  debts  and  legacies,  the  exe- 
cutor  may  have  to  pay  them  out  of  his  own  property. 


28*  OF    LAST    WILLS   AND    TESTAMENTS. 

He  must  pay  the  debts  of  the  deceased,  and  observe  the  rules 
of  priority,  according  to  the  several  degrees  which  the  law  has 
established  in  this  matter;  next  the  legatees  are  to  be  paid. x 

Executors  or  administrators  are  not  allowed  to  retain  a  part  of 
the  revenue  as  a  payment  for  their  services,  except  by  order  of  the 
Court. 

6°  A  few  practical  suggestions  on  making  a  will.  (a)  If  you  are  of 
age,  and  have  any  property  of  your  own,  make  a  will  as  soon  as 
possible  :  else  a  part  of  your  estate  might  be  wasted  in  legal  expenses. 
I)o  not  put  it  offuntil  you  are  dying  :  wills  written  when  the  testa- 
tors  are  in  extremity  are  often  unsatisfactory,  as  important  matters 
are  likely  to  be  forgotten,  and  suspicion  of  undue  influence  may  be 
aroused. 

(b)  A  will  entirely  of  your  own  handwriting  affbrds  the  best  proof 
that  it  is  genuine;  but  take  heed  that  its  legal  expressions  be  suffi- 
ciently  clear;  hence,  be  not  satisfied  with  reading  the  statute-law 
of  your  own  State  on  the  matter  of  wills,  but  consult  a  lawyer,  and 
show  him  your  draft.  After  your  will  has  been  prepared,  think  its 
provisions  over,  for  two  or  three  days  before  executing  it,  provided 
of  course  you  are  not  in  danger  of  death. 

(c)  Write  out  your  will  in  a  plain  and  clear  style ;  if  it  is  obscure, 
the  Court  may  have  difficulty  to  get  at  your  intention.  See  that  the 
words  used  by  you  not  only  convey  your  meaning,  but  that  they 
convey  no  other  meaning.  If  you  make  a  detailed  will,  be  careful 
in  the  description  of  the  property  devised  to  your  legatees.  —  When 
the  will  is  written  on  several  sheets  of  paper,  it  is  safe  to  sign  every 
sheet,  the  better  to  identify  it. 

(d)  See  whether,  in  case  your  legatee  dies  before  you,  you  wish 
his  children  or  other  representatives  to  take  his  share,  and  express 
it  clearly. 

(e)  Have  witnesses  respectable  for  their  character  and  good  stand- 
ing,  clear-headed,  honest  and  disinterested,  one  or  two  more  than 
the  number  strictly  required,  who  are  not  your  own  legatees.  Talk 
with  them  clearly  and  intelligently  upon  matters  of  local  and  per- 
sonal  interest,  so  as  to  impress  upon  them  that  you  are  perfectly 
sound  of  mind  and  free  from  all  undue  influence. 

(f )  When  once  your  will  has  been  executed,  permit  no  alteration 
of  any  sort :  but,  if  you  have  changed  your  mind,  make  rather  a 
new  instrument. 

(g)  Keep  your  will  in  such  custody  as  it  will  not  be  destroyed  or 
altered,  and  leave  a  sealed  copy  of  it  to  a  trustworthy  friend. 

1  As  for  the  order  to  be  followed  in  the  payment  of  debts  and  lega- 
cies,  see  Stephen,  vol.  II,  pag.  209-215;  and,  with  regard  to  the  United 
States,  the  various  Statutes.

XII.     Of  the  law  of  descent. 

In  the  case  of  an  intesta&y,  i.  e,  where  no  will  has  been  made,  or 
where  the  testator  has  not  disposed  of  his  whole  estate,  the  property 
or  its  residuum  has  to  be  divided  according  to  the  law  of  descent. 

i°  In  England,  a  distinction  is  to  be  made  between  real  and 
personal  estate. 

(A)  The  rules  of  descent  applicable  to  the  real  estate  of  persons 
dying  before  the  first  day  of  January,  1834,  are  as  follows  :  x 

(a)  In  every  case  the  descent  shall  be  traced  from  the purchaser ; 
now  the  word  purchaser  means  here  the  person  who  last  acquired 
the  land  otherwise  than  by  descent. 

(b)  Inheritance  shall  in  the  first  place  lineally  descend  to  the  issue 
of  the  purchaser,  in  infinitum. 

(c)  The  children  of  the  purchaser  are  preferred  to  the  grandchil- 
dren  or  remoter  issue ;  among  such  children,  males  are  preferred  to 
females,  and  an  elder  male  is  preferred  to  a  younger;  but  females 
take  together. 

(d)  The  issue  of  the  children  of  the  purchaser  represent  or  take 
the  place  of  their  deceased  parents  in  infinitum,  subject  always  to 
the  third  rule  (c). 

(e)  On  failure  of  the  issue  of  the  purchaser,  the  inheritance  shall 
descend  to  the  nearest  lineal  ancestor  then  living  in  the  preferable 
line,  —  supposing  no  issue  of  a  nearer  deceased  ancestor  in  that 
line  to  exist. 

(f)  Among  the  lineal  ancestors  of  the  purchaser,  the  paternal  line 
is  always  preferred  to  the  maternal. 

lg)  Where  an  ancestor,  to  whom,  if  living  at  the  purchaser's  death^ 
the  inheritance,  would  according  to  the  fifth  rule  (e),  descend,  dies 
before  the  purchaser,  leaving  issue,  the  issue  of  such  ancestor 
in  infinitum  shall  represent  him,  according  to  the  same  law  of  suc- 
cession  laid  down  with  respect  to  the  issue  of  the  purchaser;  but 
with  this  addition,  that  those  related  by  the  whole  blood  to  the 
purchaser,  are  preferred  to  those  related  by  the  half-blood. 

(B)  With  regard  to  the  personal  estate,  according  to  the  Statute 
of  Distributions  (22-23  Car.  II,  c.  10)  and  the  /nterstates1  Estates 
Act,  1890,  it  must  be  distributed  in  the  following  manner  : 

(a)  One-third  should  go  to  the  widow  of  the  intestate,  and  the 
residue  in  equal  proportion  to  his  children ;  or,  if  they  were  dead,  to 
their  representatives,  that  is  their  lineal  descendants;  if  there  were 
no  children  or  lineal  descendants,  then  a  moiety  is  to  go  to  the  widow 

1  These  rules  are  condensed  from  Stephen's  vol.  I,  p.  369-406,  to 
which  \ve  refer  our  readers  for  a  clear  exposition  of  the  same.

and  a  moiety  to  the  next  of  kindred  in  equal  degree, *  and  their 
representatives ;  therefore  the  father  succeeds  to  all  the  personal 
effects  of  his  children  who  die  intestate  without  wife  or  issue,  in 
exclusion  of  the  deceased;  if  the  father  be  dead,  and  any  of  the 
children  die  intestate  without  wife  or  issue,  the  mother  and  each  of 
the  brothers  or  sisters  of  the  deceased  (or  their  representatives) 
shall  divide  his  effects  in  equal  portions. 

(b)  If  no  widow  should  survive,  the  whole  estate  is  to  go  to  the 
children;  if  there  were  neither  widow  nor  children,  the  whole  is  to 
be  distributed  among  the  next  of  kin  in  equal  degree,  and  their 
representatives. 

(c)  No  children  of  the  intestate  on  whom  he  may  have  settled,  in 
his  lifetime,  any  estate  in  lands  or  pecuniary  portidn  equal  to  the 
distributive  shares  of  the  other  children,  shall  have  any  part  of  the 
surplusage  (the  remainder  of  property)  with  their  brothers  and 
sisters;  but,  if  the  estates,  so  given  them  by  way  of  advancement, 
shall  not  be  quite  equivalent  to  the  other  shares,  the  children  so 
advanced  shall  have  as  much  as  will  make  them  equal  to  their 
brothers. 

(d)  When  a  husband  dies  intestate  (after  the  ist  September,  1890) 
and  leaves  no  issue,  the  whole  estate,  real  and  personal  of  the 
deceased  now  passes  to  his  widow,  if  it  be  under  a  total  value  of 
500  pounds;  and  where  such  estate  exceeds  that  value,  she  now 
takes  500  pounds  out  of  it,  in  priority  to  all  persons  entitled  under 
the  Statutes  0/ Distribution  (as  above);  and  then,  the  residue  of 
the  personal  estate  is  distributable  according  to  the  former  law, 
that  is  to  say,  one  half  to  the  widow  and  the  remaining  one-half 
among  the  next  of  kin. 

20  In  America,  the  laws  of  descent  vary  according  to  the  Statutes 
of  the  various  States,  and,  as  changes  in  this  matter  are  f requent,  it 
is  necessary  to  take  into  consideration  the  latest  statutes.  The  only 
general  rule  is  that  the  property  goes  to  the  lawful  descendants  in 
the  direct  line,  i.  e.  to  the  children,  next  to  the  grand-children,  and 
so  on,  without  distinction  of  sex.  Where  the  descendants  are  in 
equal  degree,  each  one  receives  an  equal  share,  and  therefore  takes 
per  capita;  for  instance,  if  there  be  three  brothers,  each  one  will 
receive  one  third  of  the  inheritance.  Where  the  descendants  are  of 
different  degrees,  —  v.  g.  one  child  and  two  grand-children,  —  the 
grand  children  take  per  stirpes,  or  representation,  i.  e.  inherit  only 
such  a  share  as  their  parents  would  have  respectively  inherited.  To 
illustrate  :  A.  leaves  B.  a  son  and  two  grand-children  D.  and  E.,
